prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map depicts a downward-angled outdoor scene with brick steps on the bottom left and a paved area on the right, showing a foreground person in front of and below the camera wearer at roughly 0.4 to 1.2 metres, a second person standing to the left at about 1.5 to 2.5 metres (roughly 0.5 to 1.0 metre behind and left of the foreground person), and distant background figures in frames 2 and 3 over 10 metres away. The foreground person's head and head-mounted action camera are brightest and closest (0.3 to 0.5 metres, well within the camera wearer's arm's reach), while their torso and hands holding a small battery and strap are further down at 0.7 to 1.0 metre, and the left person's lower body and held grey backpack are at 1.5 to 2.0 metres with their upper torso cropped out of the top left edge. Both main individuals face slightly toward the left and look downward toward the objects in their hands rather than toward the camera wearer, while the foreground person's head and camera partially occlude their own upper chest and the lower legs of the person to the left. Across the 5 frames, the camera wearer's view shifts downward and right in frames 2 and 3—bringing the foreground person's head to the top-left at ~0.3 metres and revealing the distant upper-right walkway—before tilting back left and slightly further away in frames 4 and 5 as the foreground person turns their torso slightly more toward the camera wearer. Compared to RGB alone, the depth map clearly separates the foreground head and protruding camera mount from the chest below and highlights the stepped geometry on the lower left, though it becomes unreliable where the background pavement drops to uniform black in the upper right and where the foreground head saturates to pure white in frames 2 and 3.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates the foreground person on the right (~0.4 to 1.2 metres from the camera wearer), the partial person standing to the left (~1.5 to 2.5 metres away and ~0.5 to 1.0 metre to the foreground person's left), the held grey bag between them (~1.2 to 1.8 metres), and tiny distant people at the top right of frames 2 and 3 (>10 metres away). The foreground person's hands and held small device (at ~0.8 metres, within both their own and the camera wearer's arm's reach) are positioned below their torso, while the left person's hands hold the bag within their own arm's reach just to the left of the foreground person's right arm. Across the 5 frames, the masks track the relative shift as the foreground person's head moves left in frames 2 and 3 to occlude the grey bag completely in the segmentation, before moving right again in frames 4 and 5 so the bag reappears between the two people while the left person's upper body remains cropped by the top-left border. The segmentation map makes it easier than RGB alone to spot the tiny distant pedestrians at the top edge of frames 2 and 3 and delineates the exact boundary between the two adjacent people and the bag. However, it is unreliable in object classification and completeness: it leaves the foreground person's head-mounted camera unsegmented as a black hole inside their mask (or mislabels it as a turquoise 'handbag' in frame 4), alternates the grey backpack's label between 'handbag' and 'backpack' while missing it entirely in frames 2 and 3, and misclassifies the small camera battery or strap at the foreground person's waist as a 'cell phone' in frames 3 to 5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map renders 2D skeletal keypoints on a black background, consistently detecting the two magenta hands of the foreground person in the lower-centre of frames 1 through 4 and only a single hand in frame 5, at roughly 0.7 to 1.0 metre in front of and below the camera wearer (within arm's reach of both the foreground person and the camera wearer). Those hands are positioned close together in front of the foreground person's waist as they face forward-left and angle their head downward away from the camera wearer, with their left hand slightly to the right and below their right hand as the fingers manipulate the small object across the 5 frames. Across the sequence, the hand skeletons shift downward and slightly right from frame 1 to frame 3 as the camera pans, shift back left in frame 4 where a distorted yellow torso and head-keypoint cluster briefly appears over the hands, and move to the bottom right in frame 5 where the foreground person's right hand is no longer detected. The pose map makes the fine finger articulation and relative orientation of the foreground person's two opposing hands much clearer than the cluttered RGB image, where dark straps and the battery obscure the finger joints. However, the map is highly unreliable for scene-level body tracking, completely missing the full body skeleton of the foreground person in frames 1, 2, 3, and 5, collapsing their body and facial keypoints onto their hands in frame 4, and failing to detect any body or hand skeletons for the partially cropped person on the left (~1.5 to 2.5 metres away) or the distant pedestrians across all frames.
